newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda tribunal set to hear first witnesses.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda tribunal set to hear first witnesses.

text.p: The international tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide, dogged by delays and allegations of mismanagement, sits on Thursday hoping to hear evidence from witnesses for the first time.
The prosecution is expected to call witnesses in the trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), a tribunal spokesman said.

Akayesu, a former mayor in central Rwanda's Taba commune, has pleaded not guilty to charges of crimes against humanity and genocide during the killing of about 800,000 minority Tutsis and political moderates of the majority Hutu tribe between April and June 1994.
His trial was adjourned last October to allow the defence time to prepare its case but will now re-start at ICTR headquarters in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
"They will be the first witnesses brought in front of the court by the prosecution," tribunal spokesman Bocar Sy said.
"This is the first time that we will see people who will testify 'I saw this or I saw that or I saw someone giving orders to kill'," Sy said by telephone.
Witnesses likely to be fellow-residents of Taba commune who survived the genocide were being brought to Arusha under tight security, Sy said.
The U.N. tribunal had a series of false starts in 1995 with a series of adjournments on procedural grounds.

But far worse for its image was the disclosure last October that U.N. headquarters in New York had sent auditors and investigators to probe the tribunal in Arusha and its prosecution office in Kigali, the Rwandan capital.
Details of the inquiry were not made public but were linked to allegations of mismanagement.
The location of the tribunal in Arusha, a town with poor transport connections and execrable telecommunications, has further added to delays.
Defence counsel Nicolas Taingaye, a barrister from the Central African Republic, is Akayesu's third lawyer.
Sy said Taingaye was entitled to press the panel of three judges led by Senegalese presiding judge Laity Kama for a further postponement to the case.
Jurists had hoped the Arusha trials set up in November 1994 and parallel trials in The Hague for war crimes in the former Yugoslavia would show the world mass killings would not go unpunished.
Genocide trials held by Rwanda under its own genocide law threaten to overshadow the laborious ICTR process.
A Rwandan court convicted and sentenced to death two Hutus this week for genocide and crimes against humanity after a four-hour trial on December 27.
Rwanda has scheduled more trials for next week and the two men, who had no defence lawyers, were given 15 days to appeal.
The maximum sanction available to the U.N. tribunal is life imprisonment in humane conditions.

The ICTR, which had a budget of $36 million in 1996, has indicted 21 suspects of whom 13 are in custody, a tribunal spokeswoman said. Rwanda has around 90,000 Hutus in its jails accused or suspected of crimes related to the genocide.
Trials of seven other suspects have been set between February and August in Arusha.
